Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.title: 4DMemory: Benchmarking Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Memory with Harness-Augmented Agents
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.authors_text: Yanhao Jia, Yi Zhu, Yiran Zhong, Weigao Sun, Feida Zhu
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.summary: The paper introduces the 4DMemory framework and LongVideo dataset to benchmark and enhance long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning in agents, revealing significant performance improvements with the 4DMemory Harness.
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.debug_abstract: Humans efficiently process multimodal streams spanning hours to years, building persistent, fine-grained spatiotemporal memories that support reasoning about and predicting long-horizon events. In contrast, existing benchmarks focus on short- and medium-context tasks, and most foundation models struggle to preserve fine-grained information over long horizons. To evaluate and improve long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning, we introduce the LongVideo dataset and the 4DMemoryBench. LongVideo comprises about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions covering visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning across diverse context lengths. We further develop the 4DMemory Harness, which integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and a model-specific retrieval-augmented generation system. Evaluating 13 leading models, we find that standalone foundation models struggle with long-horizon tasks, while the 4DMemory Harness improves all of them by over 50\%. Compared to previous benchmark, the same models exhibit a performance drop of more than 10\% on 4DMemoryBench. We hope 4DMemory will facilitate the development of spatiotemporal agents capable of addressing complex, long-horizon tasks.

Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.title: EgoForesight: Effectively Scaling Policy Learning with Noisy Egocentric Actions
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.authors_text: Chubin Zhang, Changyuan Wang, Yirui Wang, Ao Li, Shilin Ma
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.summary: EgoForesight enhances policy learning by integrating noisy egocentric actions and robot demonstrations, improving performance and scaling through reliability-aware action learning and outcome-informed representation transfer.
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.debug_abstract: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. Egocentric videos broaden task and environment coverage, yet motion reconstruction and retargeting introduce noisy action labels. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoForesight, a vision-language-action framework that learns jointly from both sources by reducing the influence of unreliable action labels and exploiting demonstrated outcomes as complementary supervision. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source's contribution. Complementing this treatment of noisy labels, privileged-future representation distillation draws supervision from demonstrated outcomes. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. After post-training, it also achieves strong absolute performance in both simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation.

Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.title: WorldMirror: Agentic Real-to-Sim Generation of Interactive Worlds from In-the-Wild Robot Demonstrations
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.authors_text: Tianling Xu, Weijie Wan, Honghao Su, Kailun Su, Junyuan Tang
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.summary: WorldMirror is a framework that transforms real-world robot demonstrations into interactive digital twins through iterative refinement and high-fidelity scene reconstruction.
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.debug_abstract: Existing approaches for robot learning in simulation often require substantial manual effort to construct scenes and specify tasks, limiting training scalability and data diversity. Meanwhile, in-the-wild robot demonstrations naturally provide diverse and realistic observations of real-world interactions. Leveraging these demonstrations for simulation requires both high-fidelity visual reconstruction and physically consistent interactions. General-purpose agents offer flexible adaptation to diverse scenarios and strong reasoning about 3D spatial relationships, while specialized generative models provide high-fidelity reconstruction of scene appearance and geometry. We introduce WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework that constructs interactive digital twins from in-the-wild robot demonstrations. Our central idea is to formulate real-to-sim construction as the iterative refinement of an executable world program. A coding agent decomposes the observed scene, plans reconstruction steps, and orchestrates specialized image and 3D generation tools, refining the program through verification feedback. A camera-pose-anchored scene representation organizes the world into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships among the scene, objects, and robot. The agent uses this representation to diagnose and correct reconstruction errors, enabling physically consistent interaction and trajectory replay. Experiments on DROID demonstrate that WorldMirror can reconstruct visually faithful and geometrically consistent interactive worlds while preserving the physical validity of recorded robot trajectories.

Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.title: LocoManiLab: A Unified Testbed for Data, Policies, Controllers, and Deployment in Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.authors_text: Dewei Wang, Jinrui Han, Jiyuan Shi, Chenyun Zhang, Xianbo Lu
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.summary: LocoManiLab is a comprehensive testbed for humanoid loco-manipulation, facilitating data collection, policy evaluation, and deployment across diverse tasks and environments.
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.debug_abstract: Humanoid robots must coordinate locomotion and manipulation in everyday environments, yet progress is difficult to assess across differing policies, controllers, and task settings. LocoManiLab provides an integrated testbed spanning data collection and generation, policy training, evaluation, and physical deployment. Its task suite covers 234 atomic and compositional tasks across five household scene categories, supported by 51.5 hours of simulated teleoperation. The evaluation covers twelve policies with a shared controller across task and scene splits and perturbation levels, two policies across five controllers, and studies of demonstration scale and data-source mixtures. Success rates fall on unseen tasks and scenes and generally decline as visual perturbations increase, with differences in generalization and robustness across policies. For data generation, a humanoid motion generation model is fine-tuned for loco-manipulation to study the alignment of its outputs with task execution requirements and its integration into the data generation pipeline. Three simulated loco-manipulation tasks closely match real-world setups, enabling evaluation of three policies in both domains. Similar policy rankings support the reliability of simulation-based evaluation.

Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.title: Taming CoT Obfuscation in VLMs: From Mechanistic Evidence to Activation-Level Enforcement
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.authors_text: Xutao Mao, Jianing Zhu, Jinman Zhao, Tongliang Liu, Xiaowen Chu
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.summary: The paper introduces TAME, a framework that mitigates chain-of-thought obfuscation in vision-language models by regularizing internal features during reinforcement learning training, enhancing transparency and monitorability.
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs), yet it can induce chain-of-thought (CoT) obfuscation, an operational, non-intentional regime where models achieve high accuracy while producing reasoning traces that are less grounded and harder to monitor. While prior work documents this decay at the behavioral level, the underlying representational correlates of such drift remain poorly understood. In this work, we find that obfuscation is accompanied by a representational shift, where RL-induced optimization makes task-agnostic template features less separable from visually grounded content in the model's activation space. Based on this insight, we propose TAME, an activation-level intervention framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to regularize VLM internal features during RL training. Specifically, TAME utilizes an anti-obfuscation feedback loop to reduce behavioral obfuscation and applies an asymmetric SAE constraint to specific internal directions, penalizing template activations while preserving visual evidence. By directly intervening on the features associated with obfuscation, our method improves the transparency and visual grounding of reasoning traces. Experiments on the VIRL-39k and SPA-VL benchmarks across two model families show that TAME improves CoT monitorability (by up to +30.9 points on VIRL and +16.7 points on SPA-VL over GRPO), while largely preserving task accuracy and general-capability performance across four standard VLM benchmarks, with task-specific trade-offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/henrymao2004/TAME.

Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.title: CARE: Consistent Action-Response Execution for Human-Guided Robot Transport
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.authors_text: Ning Liu, Sen Shen, Zheng Li, Matthew D'Souza, Jen Jen Chung
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.summary: The CARE framework enhances human-guided robot transport by optimizing action-response execution, ensuring effective collaboration even during route mismatches, and improving performance metrics over existing methods.
Hengshuang Zhao老师实验室.debug_abstract: Human-guided collaborative transport becomes interaction-critical when the operator can continue along a route segment that is not executable by the robot--payload system. In this regime, operator motion is not an exogenous reference: it simultaneously communicates a persistent route tendency and adapts to the robot's realized progress. A common modular formulation predicts one operator future from observation history, scores multiple robot proposals against that shared forecast, and then modifies the selected command for local feasibility. This can compare candidates under responses they would not induce and can condition prediction on an action that is never executed. We formulate local control over executable-action-indexed joint human--robot transitions and instantiate it in Consistent Action--Response Execution (CARE). Each nominal proposal or bounded alternative is first mapped to an executable action; that same action conditions the route-aligned operator-response prediction, the matched robot--operator rollout, and a fixed interaction utility for candidate selection. Bounded reciprocal refinement handles transient route--feasibility mismatch, whereas persistent progress loss replaces the nominal proposal with a progress-oriented recovery proposal while retaining the same downstream executable-action-conditioned evaluation. Across training and held-out maps, CARE preserves near-saturated performance when the indicated route remains locally usable and achieves the highest observed success and service availability when the operator can continue but the robot must detour. It also yields lower jerk-proxy values and measured controller latency than dynamic-window and Timed Elastic Band baselines. Factorial ablations distinguish reciprocal refinement from progress recovery, delayed-response tests probe temporal mismatch, and an indoor deployment demonstrates physical executability.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: From Freehand Demonstrations to Autonomous Robotic Ultrasound: An Anatomy-Anchored Learning Framework
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yuan Bi, Fangxu Han, Ye Su, Yiping Zhou, Zhongliang Jiang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper presents an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework for robotic ultrasound that enhances scanning success rates and efficiency through anatomical guidance and multimodal demonstrations.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Ultrasound imaging is highly operator-dependent, motivating robotic systems that reproduce expert scanning skills consistently. These skills involve coordinated interpretation of anatomical landmarks, ultrasound images, and probe-tissue interactions that are difficult to encode in hand-designed control strategies. Imitation learning offers an alternative, but its observation and action representations should reflect the anatomically structured nature of scanning. We propose an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework that combines anatomy-guided probe placement with learned ultrasound navigation. The placement module identifies a task-specific anatomical starting point from external visual observations and establishes the initial probe pose as the reference frame for scanning. A flow-based policy then generates scanning motions from anchor-relative probe poses, ultrasound images, probe-mounted camera views, and contact forces, while a termination head predicts task completion. This avoids continuous reliance on third-person vision and reduces dependence on the robot-patient configuration. A handheld acquisition platform enables multimodal demonstrations to be collected during natural freehand scanning without a robot. On 16 unseen participants, task success reaches 96%, 94%, 88%, and 94% for kidney, gallbladder, and liver standard-plane acquisition and radial artery sweeping, respectively. Compared with a fine-tuned pi_0 model, success on the abdominal tasks improves by 10-42 percentage points, with lower time-to-target, peak contact force, and trajectory jerk. Ablations support the complementary roles of anatomical anchoring, egocentric vision, and force feedback. End-to-end trials with automatic placement achieve 90-100% success, and the policies transfer without retraining to a second robot with 83-100% success.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Do Robotic World Models Really Follow Actions? Diagnosing and Aligning Action-Conditioned Generation for Policy Learning
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Sixiang Chen, Jiaming Liu, Jixian Wu, Yichen Guo, Tinghao Wang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper introduces WorldEcho and WorldSync to evaluate and improve action-conditioned world models, enhancing their reliability for robotic policy learning by aligning generated futures with actual actions.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Action-conditioned world models increasingly serve as learned simulators for robotic policy improvement, yet their reliability rests on an unverified assumption: generated futures faithfully reflect the consequences of arbitrary valid actions. Systematic evaluation against action-specific ground truth remains limited beyond expert demonstrations. To address this gap, we introduce WorldEcho, which evaluates action following over a broader action distribution through visual integrity and SE(3) end-effector trajectory alignment. Our diagnosis shows that expert-trained models perform better on demonstrated actions but struggle with off-expert trajectories, producing motion inconsistent with the commanded actions or visually invalid rollouts. To mitigate these failures, we propose WorldSync, which broadens action coverage, grounds intermediate video representations in action-induced robot dynamics through an Action-Forcing Expert, and aligns predicted and ground-truth changes under action interventions. Experiments show that WorldSync reduces integrity-gated error on RoboTwin and, when used for iterative policy improvement, yields higher success rates in simulation and on real robots.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Unified Condition-Action Modeling for Accurate One-Step Action Generation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xinyu Zhou, Zikun Cai, Kuangji Zuo, Gen Li, Boyu Ma
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: UCA-Flow introduces a unified condition-action modeling framework that enhances one-step action generation accuracy and speed by jointly representing conditions and actions in a shared token space.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Robot manipulation requires policies that are both accurate and efficient, as robot control must respond to changing observations under tight latency constraints. Recent diffusion and flow policies are promising, but they often treat conditions as auxiliary signals rather than jointly evolving them with action trajectories. We find that this limitation can be effectively mitigated by a simple yet effective unified condition-action modeling design that represents conditions and actions in a shared token space, allowing a compact model to achieve high performance while improving both inference speed and accuracy. Therefore, we propose UCA-Flow, a unified condition-action modeling framework for accurate one-step action generation. Our method unifies observation conditions, timestep conditions, interval conditions, and action tokens into a single sequence, and processes them with a Unified Condition-Action Transformer for joint condition-action representation learning. As a result, condition representations are dynamically reconstructed according to the current generation stage, highlighting information most relevant for action refinement. Furthermore, we introduce an improved dual-pass supervision scheme over $u$ and $v$ for stronger optimization of unified condition-action modeling. UCA-Flow achieves an average success rate of 86.4%, improving over the strongest baseline by 7.5 percentage points, with a task-averaged inference latency of $3.0$ ms. It achieves $43.9\times$ and $32.2\times$ speedups over DP3 and Simple DP3, and remains $4.2\times$ and $2.2\times$ faster than one-step FlowPolicy and MP1, respectively. Project page: https://uca-policy.github.io/UCA.github.io/

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: SetCon: Towards Open-Ended Referring Segmentation via Set-Level Concept Prediction
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Zhixiong Zhang, Yizhuo Li, Shuangrui Ding, Yuhang Zang, Shengyuan Ding
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: SetCon introduces a novel approach to open-ended referring segmentation by leveraging set-level concept prediction for improved pixel-level mask decoding, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Referring segmentation grounds natural-language queries to pixel-level masks, but extending it to complex scenarios with multiple instances, cross-category groups, or open-ended target sets remains challenging. Previous Large Vision Language Model (LVLM)-based methods represent referred targets with one or more special tokens sequentially, treating multiple targets as separate outputs rather than a coherent set and offering little incentive to capture set-level properties such as completeness and mutual exclusivity. We reformulate open-ended referring segmentation as explicit set-level concept prediction and propose Set-Concept Segmentation (SetCon), which uses LVLM-generated natural-language concepts, instead of segmentation-specific tokens, as semantic conditions for joint mask-set decoding. A hierarchical semantic decomposition first predicts a shared set-level concept defining the target scope and then refines it into fine-grained concept groups aligned with target subsets. To support this, a two-stage annotation pipeline augments existing reasoning segmentation datasets with hierarchical semantic supervision (236k samples, 784k concept phrases). SetCon achieves state-of-the-art results on image benchmarks (+3.3 gIoU on gRefCOCO, +12.1 gIoU on MUSE), with margins that grow as the number of referred targets increases. The concept interface also transfers to video under a detect-and-track setting, yielding new state-of-the-art results on seven referring video benchmarks, including +10.9 J&F on MeViS and +12.4 J&F on Ref-SeCVOS.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: VORL-EXPLORE: A Hybrid Learning Planning Approach to Multi-Robot Exploration in Dynamic Environments
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Ning Liu, Sen Shen, Zheng Li, Sheng Liu, Dongkun Han
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: VORL-EXPLORE enhances multi-robot exploration in dynamic environments by integrating execution awareness into planning, improving efficiency and safety through a fidelity-based allocation and navigation strategy.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Hierarchical multi-robot exploration decouples frontier allocation from local navigation, making systems brittle in dynamic environments. Without awareness of execution difficulty, allocators may send robots toward frontiers whose routes are congested or unsafe, causing bottlenecks, oscillatory replanning, and redundant coverage. We propose VORL-EXPLORE, a hybrid learning and planning framework that makes exploration execution-aware through execution fidelity, an estimate of local navigability and execution reliability. This fidelity score is used to penalize risky or crowded frontiers in a fidelity-coupled Voronoi allocation objective with inter-robot repulsion, and to arbitrate between global $A^*$ guidance and a reactive reinforcement learning policy during navigation. As a result, robots follow efficient global plans in reliable regions and rely more on safer local reactions in crowded or changing areas. The fidelity model is recalibrated using self-supervised pseudo-labels derived from recent progress and safety outcomes. Quantitative experiments on randomized dynamic grids and an ablation under severe traffic show higher success rates, shorter exploration lengths, and lower inter-robot coverage overlap. A Gazebo factory scenario is included as a deployment illustration. The source code is available at https://github.com/21ning/VORL-EXPLORE.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: MDMR-Bench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Multi-Reference Image Generation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Bowen Zheng, Jintao Lin, Changheng Yi, Haoran Yang, Binxiao Huang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: MDMR-Bench introduces a comprehensive multi-dimensional benchmark for evaluating multi-reference image generation models, enhancing assessment through structured checklists and diverse challenge dimensions.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Image generation models have rapidly advanced, with many models now supporting generation conditioned on multiple reference images and textual instructions. Such models enable a wide range of applications, including entity fusion and attribute transfer across images. However, existing benchmarks for multi-reference image generation rely on limited evaluation dimensions and fail to capture the diverse challenges of the task. To address this limitation, we propose MDMR-Bench, a Multi-Dimensional benchmark for Multi-Reference image generation. MDMR-Bench is organized around representative capability settings and consists of multiple evaluation subsets spanning diverse dimensions of multi-reference image generation, including (1) common entity fusion and attribute transfer, (2) multi-element extraction from a single image, (3) infographic manipulation, and (4) visual reasoning-intensive generation. This design enables systematic analysis of model capabilities and failure modes across different challenge dimensions. Furthermore, to achieve more reliable and interpretable evaluation, we introduce a checklist-based evaluation protocol that decomposes generation quality into fine-grained evaluation aspects. Instead of relying solely on holistic scoring, our framework uses structured checklists composed of both global-level and atomic-level queries, enabling more diagnostic assessment of model performance. By benchmarking both open-source and proprietary models, we demonstrate that MDMR-Bench provides fine-grained insights into model performance across different dimensions. The dataset and code are publicly available.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Are Frontier VLM Agents Ready to Be Robot Generalists? An Empirical Study with the Embodied Agent Arena
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Haojian Huang, Pukun Zhao, Zexi Li, Yehang Zhang, Yangkai Wei
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This study evaluates ten frontier vision-language models in the Embodied Agent Arena, revealing strengths in spatial reasoning but significant weaknesses in planning and manipulation for robot generalist tasks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: A robot generalist must interpret a scene, act on it, and satisfy every condition of a task. Beneath these averages, similar geometric errors conceal different scale and shape distortions, and valid region estimates need not identify usable action points. During execution, agents can achieve early subgoals yet lose object control, bind an action to the wrong receiving region, or stop before the required physical state holds. Additional computation does not uniformly resolve these failures: code repair can restore execution without completing the task, while self-review can reverse correct judgments. Failure costs also differ: the strongest planners concentrate failed-token expenditure in prolonged body-control tasks, whereas other models fail broadly across procedures. Matched traces show how successful recovery uses feedback to restore a missing prerequisite and advance the remaining task.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: LocoManiLab: A Unified Testbed for Data, Policies, Controllers, and Deployment in Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Dewei Wang, Jinrui Han, Jiyuan Shi, Chenyun Zhang, Xianbo Lu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: LocoManiLab is a comprehensive testbed for humanoid loco-manipulation, facilitating data collection, policy evaluation, and deployment across diverse tasks and environments.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Humanoid robots must coordinate locomotion and manipulation in everyday environments, yet progress is difficult to assess across differing policies, controllers, and task settings. LocoManiLab provides an integrated testbed spanning data collection and generation, policy training, evaluation, and physical deployment. Its task suite covers 234 atomic and compositional tasks across five household scene categories, supported by 51.5 hours of simulated teleoperation. The evaluation covers twelve policies with a shared controller across task and scene splits and perturbation levels, two policies across five controllers, and studies of demonstration scale and data-source mixtures. Success rates fall on unseen tasks and scenes and generally decline as visual perturbations increase, with differences in generalization and robustness across policies. For data generation, a humanoid motion generation model is fine-tuned for loco-manipulation to study the alignment of its outputs with task execution requirements and its integration into the data generation pipeline. Three simulated loco-manipulation tasks closely match real-world setups, enabling evaluation of three policies in both domains. Similar policy rankings support the reliability of simulation-based evaluation.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Taming CoT Obfuscation in VLMs: From Mechanistic Evidence to Activation-Level Enforcement
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xutao Mao, Jianing Zhu, Jinman Zhao, Tongliang Liu, Xiaowen Chu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper introduces TAME, a framework that mitigates chain-of-thought obfuscation in vision-language models by regularizing internal features during reinforcement learning training, enhancing transparency and monitorability.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs), yet it can induce chain-of-thought (CoT) obfuscation, an operational, non-intentional regime where models achieve high accuracy while producing reasoning traces that are less grounded and harder to monitor. While prior work documents this decay at the behavioral level, the underlying representational correlates of such drift remain poorly understood. In this work, we find that obfuscation is accompanied by a representational shift, where RL-induced optimization makes task-agnostic template features less separable from visually grounded content in the model's activation space. Based on this insight, we propose TAME, an activation-level intervention framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to regularize VLM internal features during RL training. Specifically, TAME utilizes an anti-obfuscation feedback loop to reduce behavioral obfuscation and applies an asymmetric SAE constraint to specific internal directions, penalizing template activations while preserving visual evidence. By directly intervening on the features associated with obfuscation, our method improves the transparency and visual grounding of reasoning traces. Experiments on the VIRL-39k and SPA-VL benchmarks across two model families show that TAME improves CoT monitorability (by up to +30.9 points on VIRL and +16.7 points on SPA-VL over GRPO), while largely preserving task accuracy and general-capability performance across four standard VLM benchmarks, with task-specific trade-offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/henrymao2004/TAME.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: CARE: Consistent Action-Response Execution for Human-Guided Robot Transport
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Ning Liu, Sen Shen, Zheng Li, Matthew D'Souza, Jen Jen Chung
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The CARE framework enhances human-guided robot transport by optimizing action-response execution, ensuring effective collaboration even during route mismatches, and improving performance metrics over existing methods.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Human-guided collaborative transport becomes interaction-critical when the operator can continue along a route segment that is not executable by the robot--payload system. In this regime, operator motion is not an exogenous reference: it simultaneously communicates a persistent route tendency and adapts to the robot's realized progress. A common modular formulation predicts one operator future from observation history, scores multiple robot proposals against that shared forecast, and then modifies the selected command for local feasibility. This can compare candidates under responses they would not induce and can condition prediction on an action that is never executed. We formulate local control over executable-action-indexed joint human--robot transitions and instantiate it in Consistent Action--Response Execution (CARE). Each nominal proposal or bounded alternative is first mapped to an executable action; that same action conditions the route-aligned operator-response prediction, the matched robot--operator rollout, and a fixed interaction utility for candidate selection. Bounded reciprocal refinement handles transient route--feasibility mismatch, whereas persistent progress loss replaces the nominal proposal with a progress-oriented recovery proposal while retaining the same downstream executable-action-conditioned evaluation. Across training and held-out maps, CARE preserves near-saturated performance when the indicated route remains locally usable and achieves the highest observed success and service availability when the operator can continue but the robot must detour. It also yields lower jerk-proxy values and measured controller latency than dynamic-window and Timed Elastic Band baselines. Factorial ablations distinguish reciprocal refinement from progress recovery, delayed-response tests probe temporal mismatch, and an indoor deployment demonstrates physical executability.

OpenDriveLab.title: From Freehand Demonstrations to Autonomous Robotic Ultrasound: An Anatomy-Anchored Learning Framework
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yuan Bi, Fangxu Han, Ye Su, Yiping Zhou, Zhongliang Jiang
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper presents an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework for robotic ultrasound that enhances scanning success rates and efficiency through anatomical guidance and multimodal demonstrations.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Ultrasound imaging is highly operator-dependent, motivating robotic systems that reproduce expert scanning skills consistently. These skills involve coordinated interpretation of anatomical landmarks, ultrasound images, and probe-tissue interactions that are difficult to encode in hand-designed control strategies. Imitation learning offers an alternative, but its observation and action representations should reflect the anatomically structured nature of scanning. We propose an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework that combines anatomy-guided probe placement with learned ultrasound navigation. The placement module identifies a task-specific anatomical starting point from external visual observations and establishes the initial probe pose as the reference frame for scanning. A flow-based policy then generates scanning motions from anchor-relative probe poses, ultrasound images, probe-mounted camera views, and contact forces, while a termination head predicts task completion. This avoids continuous reliance on third-person vision and reduces dependence on the robot-patient configuration. A handheld acquisition platform enables multimodal demonstrations to be collected during natural freehand scanning without a robot. On 16 unseen participants, task success reaches 96%, 94%, 88%, and 94% for kidney, gallbladder, and liver standard-plane acquisition and radial artery sweeping, respectively. Compared with a fine-tuned pi_0 model, success on the abdominal tasks improves by 10-42 percentage points, with lower time-to-target, peak contact force, and trajectory jerk. Ablations support the complementary roles of anatomical anchoring, egocentric vision, and force feedback. End-to-end trials with automatic placement achieve 90-100% success, and the policies transfer without retraining to a second robot with 83-100% success.

OpenDriveLab.title: Do Robotic World Models Really Follow Actions? Diagnosing and Aligning Action-Conditioned Generation for Policy Learning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Sixiang Chen, Jiaming Liu, Jixian Wu, Yichen Guo, Tinghao Wang
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper introduces WorldEcho and WorldSync to evaluate and improve action-conditioned world models, enhancing their reliability for robotic policy learning by aligning generated futures with actual actions.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Action-conditioned world models increasingly serve as learned simulators for robotic policy improvement, yet their reliability rests on an unverified assumption: generated futures faithfully reflect the consequences of arbitrary valid actions. Systematic evaluation against action-specific ground truth remains limited beyond expert demonstrations. To address this gap, we introduce WorldEcho, which evaluates action following over a broader action distribution through visual integrity and SE(3) end-effector trajectory alignment. Our diagnosis shows that expert-trained models perform better on demonstrated actions but struggle with off-expert trajectories, producing motion inconsistent with the commanded actions or visually invalid rollouts. To mitigate these failures, we propose WorldSync, which broadens action coverage, grounds intermediate video representations in action-induced robot dynamics through an Action-Forcing Expert, and aligns predicted and ground-truth changes under action interventions. Experiments show that WorldSync reduces integrity-gated error on RoboTwin and, when used for iterative policy improvement, yields higher success rates in simulation and on real robots.

OpenDriveLab.title: Unified Condition-Action Modeling for Accurate One-Step Action Generation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Xinyu Zhou, Zikun Cai, Kuangji Zuo, Gen Li, Boyu Ma
OpenDriveLab.summary: UCA-Flow introduces a unified condition-action modeling framework that enhances one-step action generation accuracy and speed by jointly representing conditions and actions in a shared token space.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Robot manipulation requires policies that are both accurate and efficient, as robot control must respond to changing observations under tight latency constraints. Recent diffusion and flow policies are promising, but they often treat conditions as auxiliary signals rather than jointly evolving them with action trajectories. We find that this limitation can be effectively mitigated by a simple yet effective unified condition-action modeling design that represents conditions and actions in a shared token space, allowing a compact model to achieve high performance while improving both inference speed and accuracy. Therefore, we propose UCA-Flow, a unified condition-action modeling framework for accurate one-step action generation. Our method unifies observation conditions, timestep conditions, interval conditions, and action tokens into a single sequence, and processes them with a Unified Condition-Action Transformer for joint condition-action representation learning. As a result, condition representations are dynamically reconstructed according to the current generation stage, highlighting information most relevant for action refinement. Furthermore, we introduce an improved dual-pass supervision scheme over $u$ and $v$ for stronger optimization of unified condition-action modeling. UCA-Flow achieves an average success rate of 86.4%, improving over the strongest baseline by 7.5 percentage points, with a task-averaged inference latency of $3.0$ ms. It achieves $43.9\times$ and $32.2\times$ speedups over DP3 and Simple DP3, and remains $4.2\times$ and $2.2\times$ faster than one-step FlowPolicy and MP1, respectively. Project page: https://uca-policy.github.io/UCA.github.io/

OpenDriveLab.title: SetCon: Towards Open-Ended Referring Segmentation via Set-Level Concept Prediction
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Zhixiong Zhang, Yizhuo Li, Shuangrui Ding, Yuhang Zang, Shengyuan Ding
OpenDriveLab.summary: SetCon introduces a novel approach to open-ended referring segmentation by leveraging set-level concept prediction for improved pixel-level mask decoding, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Referring segmentation grounds natural-language queries to pixel-level masks, but extending it to complex scenarios with multiple instances, cross-category groups, or open-ended target sets remains challenging. Previous Large Vision Language Model (LVLM)-based methods represent referred targets with one or more special tokens sequentially, treating multiple targets as separate outputs rather than a coherent set and offering little incentive to capture set-level properties such as completeness and mutual exclusivity. We reformulate open-ended referring segmentation as explicit set-level concept prediction and propose Set-Concept Segmentation (SetCon), which uses LVLM-generated natural-language concepts, instead of segmentation-specific tokens, as semantic conditions for joint mask-set decoding. A hierarchical semantic decomposition first predicts a shared set-level concept defining the target scope and then refines it into fine-grained concept groups aligned with target subsets. To support this, a two-stage annotation pipeline augments existing reasoning segmentation datasets with hierarchical semantic supervision (236k samples, 784k concept phrases). SetCon achieves state-of-the-art results on image benchmarks (+3.3 gIoU on gRefCOCO, +12.1 gIoU on MUSE), with margins that grow as the number of referred targets increases. The concept interface also transfers to video under a detect-and-track setting, yielding new state-of-the-art results on seven referring video benchmarks, including +10.9 J&F on MeViS and +12.4 J&F on Ref-SeCVOS.

OpenDriveLab.title: VORL-EXPLORE: A Hybrid Learning Planning Approach to Multi-Robot Exploration in Dynamic Environments
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Ning Liu, Sen Shen, Zheng Li, Sheng Liu, Dongkun Han
OpenDriveLab.summary: VORL-EXPLORE enhances multi-robot exploration in dynamic environments by integrating execution awareness into planning, improving efficiency and safety through a fidelity-based allocation and navigation strategy.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Hierarchical multi-robot exploration decouples frontier allocation from local navigation, making systems brittle in dynamic environments. Without awareness of execution difficulty, allocators may send robots toward frontiers whose routes are congested or unsafe, causing bottlenecks, oscillatory replanning, and redundant coverage. We propose VORL-EXPLORE, a hybrid learning and planning framework that makes exploration execution-aware through execution fidelity, an estimate of local navigability and execution reliability. This fidelity score is used to penalize risky or crowded frontiers in a fidelity-coupled Voronoi allocation objective with inter-robot repulsion, and to arbitrate between global $A^*$ guidance and a reactive reinforcement learning policy during navigation. As a result, robots follow efficient global plans in reliable regions and rely more on safer local reactions in crowded or changing areas. The fidelity model is recalibrated using self-supervised pseudo-labels derived from recent progress and safety outcomes. Quantitative experiments on randomized dynamic grids and an ablation under severe traffic show higher success rates, shorter exploration lengths, and lower inter-robot coverage overlap. A Gazebo factory scenario is included as a deployment illustration. The source code is available at https://github.com/21ning/VORL-EXPLORE.

OpenDriveLab.title: MDMR-Bench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Multi-Reference Image Generation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Bowen Zheng, Jintao Lin, Changheng Yi, Haoran Yang, Binxiao Huang
OpenDriveLab.summary: MDMR-Bench introduces a comprehensive multi-dimensional benchmark for evaluating multi-reference image generation models, enhancing assessment through structured checklists and diverse challenge dimensions.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Image generation models have rapidly advanced, with many models now supporting generation conditioned on multiple reference images and textual instructions. Such models enable a wide range of applications, including entity fusion and attribute transfer across images. However, existing benchmarks for multi-reference image generation rely on limited evaluation dimensions and fail to capture the diverse challenges of the task. To address this limitation, we propose MDMR-Bench, a Multi-Dimensional benchmark for Multi-Reference image generation. MDMR-Bench is organized around representative capability settings and consists of multiple evaluation subsets spanning diverse dimensions of multi-reference image generation, including (1) common entity fusion and attribute transfer, (2) multi-element extraction from a single image, (3) infographic manipulation, and (4) visual reasoning-intensive generation. This design enables systematic analysis of model capabilities and failure modes across different challenge dimensions. Furthermore, to achieve more reliable and interpretable evaluation, we introduce a checklist-based evaluation protocol that decomposes generation quality into fine-grained evaluation aspects. Instead of relying solely on holistic scoring, our framework uses structured checklists composed of both global-level and atomic-level queries, enabling more diagnostic assessment of model performance. By benchmarking both open-source and proprietary models, we demonstrate that MDMR-Bench provides fine-grained insights into model performance across different dimensions. The dataset and code are publicly available.

OpenDriveLab.title: Are Frontier VLM Agents Ready to Be Robot Generalists? An Empirical Study with the Embodied Agent Arena
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Haojian Huang, Pukun Zhao, Zexi Li, Yehang Zhang, Yangkai Wei
OpenDriveLab.summary: This study evaluates ten frontier vision-language models in the Embodied Agent Arena, revealing strengths in spatial reasoning but significant weaknesses in planning and manipulation for robot generalist tasks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: A robot generalist must interpret a scene, act on it, and satisfy every condition of a task. How far do frontier vision-language models (VLMs) meet these demands? We introduce Embodied Agent Arena, evaluating ten VLM agents across Geometry, Spatial Reasoning, Affordance, Task Planning, and Manipulation. Its 1,000 cases combine 32 established sources with GeoProbe, our 168-case benchmark for camera, motion, depth, and scale estimation. A minimal harness leaves task decisions to the model through source-native interfaces. Closed-weight models lead all five domains, whereas open-weight VLMs show useful spatial reasoning but substantially lower planning and manipulation success. Beneath these averages, similar geometric errors conceal different scale and shape distortions, and valid region estimates need not identify usable action points. During execution, agents can achieve early subgoals yet lose object control, bind an action to the wrong receiving region, or stop before the required physical state holds. Additional computation does not uniformly resolve these failures: code repair can restore execution without completing the task, while self-review can reverse correct judgments. Failure costs also differ: the strongest planners concentrate failed-token expenditure in prolonged body-control tasks, whereas other models fail broadly across procedures. Matched traces show how successful recovery uses feedback to restore a missing prerequisite and advance the remaining task.

OpenDriveLab.title: When to Stop Penalizing Actions? Martingale GRPO for VLA Reinforcement Learning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Zongyao Zhao, Cheng-Jie Zhao, Ruihang Jiang, Bing Zheng, Zhaolin Wang
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper introduces Martingale GRPO (MART-GRPO), which optimizes failure feedback in VLA reinforcement learning by selectively truncating error contributions to enhance success rates.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: A failed vision-language-action (VLA) rollout does not imply that every action contributed to failure. Yet in group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), a single trajectory-level advantage is assigned to all actions in a rollout. Potentially useful recovery attempts can thus be penalized alongside the errors they aim to correct. Ideal stopping conditions for failure feedback are characterized using success-probability and policy-score martingales. At these stops, the removed gradient contribution has zero conditional expectation given the retained information. Truncation therefore preserves the expectation of a reference GRPO group-gradient estimator and can reduce its covariance. One such stop occurs when the conditional probability of success is zero, motivating error and recovery cues for selecting candidate feedback boundaries. Martingale GRPO (MART-GRPO) is introduced with a vision-language model (VLM) for event-guided truncation. The VLM is fine-tuned on our annotated training set using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The last visible error without observed recovery is localized by the frozen VLM in complete rollout videos. Failure feedback is retained through the selected error interval and removed afterward, while successful-rollout loss terms and original loss normalization are preserved. For retrospective boundaries, changes in expectation and variance are analyzed to assess departures from ideal stopping. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 show that MART-GRPO improves success rates over full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.

OpenDriveLab.title: 4DMemory: Benchmarking Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Memory with Harness-Augmented Agents
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yanhao Jia, Yi Zhu, Yiran Zhong, Weigao Sun, Feida Zhu
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper introduces the 4DMemory framework and LongVideo dataset to benchmark and enhance long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning in agents, revealing significant performance improvements with the 4DMemory Harness.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Humans efficiently process multimodal streams spanning hours to years, building persistent, fine-grained spatiotemporal memories that support reasoning about and predicting long-horizon events. In contrast, existing benchmarks focus on short- and medium-context tasks, and most foundation models struggle to preserve fine-grained information over long horizons. To evaluate and improve long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning, we introduce the LongVideo dataset and the 4DMemoryBench. LongVideo comprises about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions covering visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning across diverse context lengths. We further develop the 4DMemory Harness, which integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and a model-specific retrieval-augmented generation system. Evaluating 13 leading models, we find that standalone foundation models struggle with long-horizon tasks, while the 4DMemory Harness improves all of them by over 50\%. Compared to previous benchmark, the same models exhibit a performance drop of more than 10\% on 4DMemoryBench. We hope 4DMemory will facilitate the development of spatiotemporal agents capable of addressing complex, long-horizon tasks.

OpenDriveLab.title: EgoForesight: Effectively Scaling Policy Learning with Noisy Egocentric Actions
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Chubin Zhang, Changyuan Wang, Yirui Wang, Ao Li, Shilin Ma
OpenDriveLab.summary: EgoForesight enhances policy learning by integrating noisy egocentric actions and robot demonstrations, improving performance and scaling through reliability-aware action learning and outcome-informed representation transfer.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. Egocentric videos broaden task and environment coverage, yet motion reconstruction and retargeting introduce noisy action labels. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoForesight, a vision-language-action framework that learns jointly from both sources by reducing the influence of unreliable action labels and exploiting demonstrated outcomes as complementary supervision. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source's contribution. Complementing this treatment of noisy labels, privileged-future representation distillation draws supervision from demonstrated outcomes. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. After post-training, it also achieves strong absolute performance in both simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation.

OpenDriveLab.title: WorldMirror: Agentic Real-to-Sim Generation of Interactive Worlds from In-the-Wild Robot Demonstrations
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Tianling Xu, Weijie Wan, Honghao Su, Kailun Su, Junyuan Tang
OpenDriveLab.summary: WorldMirror is a framework that transforms real-world robot demonstrations into interactive digital twins through iterative refinement and high-fidelity scene reconstruction.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Existing approaches for robot learning in simulation often require substantial manual effort to construct scenes and specify tasks, limiting training scalability and data diversity. Meanwhile, in-the-wild robot demonstrations naturally provide diverse and realistic observations of real-world interactions. Leveraging these demonstrations for simulation requires both high-fidelity visual reconstruction and physically consistent interactions. General-purpose agents offer flexible adaptation to diverse scenarios and strong reasoning about 3D spatial relationships, while specialized generative models provide high-fidelity reconstruction of scene appearance and geometry. We introduce WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework that constructs interactive digital twins from in-the-wild robot demonstrations. Our central idea is to formulate real-to-sim construction as the iterative refinement of an executable world program. A coding agent decomposes the observed scene, plans reconstruction steps, and orchestrates specialized image and 3D generation tools, refining the program through verification feedback. A camera-pose-anchored scene representation organizes the world into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships among the scene, objects, and robot. The agent uses this representation to diagnose and correct reconstruction errors, enabling physically consistent interaction and trajectory replay. Experiments on DROID demonstrate that WorldMirror can reconstruct visually faithful and geometrically consistent interactive worlds while preserving the physical validity of recorded robot trajectories.

具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).title: Beyond Pattern Matching in 3D MLLMs: Part-Level Functional Reasoning for Generalizable Recognition
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).authors_text: Weihong Li, Hao Jiang, Yaohua Zha, Tao Dai, Shu-Tao Xia
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).summary: The paper introduces PFIR, a method enhancing 3D object recognition by employing part-level functional reasoning, significantly improving accuracy on geometrically ambiguous objects.
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).debug_abstract: 3D MLLMs recognize objects via pattern matching, which fails when geometrically similar objects require functional reasoning to disambiguate (e.g., dresser vs. wardrobe). Our per-sample Geometric Confusion Score (GCS) exposes this failure: baseline accuracy is 33.7% on ModelNet40's most ambiguous 20% versus 84.0% on its least ambiguous 20%. We identify a function-as-annotation pattern, in which functional language decorates a known identity instead of supporting inference, and hypothesize that reversing this information flow should concentrate improvements on the most ambiguous samples. PFIR (Part-level Functional Inference for Recognition) reverses that flow. Built on PartNeXt part segmentation, its data pipeline produces 507K QA pairs with functional CoTs (geometry $\to$ function $\to$ identity), and its progressive curriculum culminates in dual-objective GRPO: strict functional reasoning and descriptive grounding for Objaverse's diverse distribution. The two RL objectives yield nearly orthogonal task vectors ($\cos = 0.056$), enabling composition via Task Arithmetic. 具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).title: MirrorCraft: Paired Evaluation under Hidden Rule Changes in Minecraft
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).authors_text: Jianxin Gao, Beini Hu, Runze Li, Hongjian Fang, Wanli Peng

具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).debug_abstract: With the rapid progress of large language models (LLMs), an interesting question has emerged: how do LLM-based agents perform in Minecraft? 具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).authors_text: Zongyao Zhao, Cheng-Jie Zhao, Ruihang Jiang, Bing Zheng, Zhaolin Wang

具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).debug_abstract: A failed vision-language-action (VLA) rollout does not imply that every action contributed to failure. Yet in group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), a single trajectory-level advantage is assigned to all actions in a rollout. Potentially useful recovery attempts can thus be penalized alongside the errors they aim to correct. Ideal stopping conditions for failure feedback are characterized using success-probability and policy-score martingales. At these stops, the removed gradient contribution has zero conditional expectation given the retained information. Truncation therefore preserves the expectation of a reference GRPO group-gradient estimator and can reduce its covariance. One such stop occurs when the conditional probability of success is zero, motivating error and recovery cues for selecting candidate feedback boundaries. Martingale GRPO (MART-GRPO) is introduced with a vision-language model (VLM) for event-guided truncation. The VLM is fine-tuned on our annotated training set using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The last visible error without observed recovery is localized by the frozen VLM in complete rollout videos. Failure feedback is retained through the selected error interval and removed afterward, while successful-rollout loss terms and original loss normalization are preserved. For retrospective boundaries, changes in expectation and variance are analyzed to assess departures from ideal stopping. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 show that MART-GRPO improves success rates over full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.

具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).title: EgoForesight: Effectively Scaling Policy Learning with Noisy Egocentric Actions
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).authors_text: Chubin Zhang, Changyuan Wang, Yirui Wang, Ao Li, Shilin Ma
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).summary: EgoForesight enhances policy learning by integrating noisy egocentric actions and robot demonstrations, improving performance and scaling through reliability-aware action learning and outcome-informed representation transfer.
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).debug_abstract: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source's contribution. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. 具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).authors_text: Xiao Tan, Yixuan Wang, Zhexi Wang, Wenzhen Yuan
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).summary: FORCA is a coding agent that uses visual and force/torque inputs to autonomously generate Python programs for effective contact-rich robot manipulation without prior demonstrations or training.
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).debug_abstract: Coding agents can translate language instructions into robot programs. For contact-rich manipulation, a key challenge is to generate and refine control logic that responds to physical interaction. We present FORCA, a coding agent that takes visual observations and wrist force/torque (F/T) measurements as input to write Python programs for contact probing and force-responsive motion. Between executions, the agent inspects force records alongside visual outcomes to diagnose failures and revise both motion and force-feedback control logic. FORCA requires no demonstrations, task-specific training, or simulation. Across five real-robot tasks, we demonstrate its effectiveness in three forms of contact-rich manipulation: improving manipulation accuracy, adapting to changes in object or surface properties, and regulating contact under surface variation and object motion. Compared with a vision-only variant of the same agent, FORCA improves grasp accuracy and task success and reduces contact loss in wiping and peeling.

具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).title: WorldMirror: Agentic Real-to-Sim Generation of Interactive Worlds from In-the-Wild Robot Demonstrations
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).authors_text: Tianling Xu, Weijie Wan, Honghao Su, Kailun Su, Junyuan Tang
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).summary: WorldMirror is a framework that transforms real-world robot demonstrations into interactive digital twins through iterative refinement and high-fidelity scene reconstruction.
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).debug_abstract: Existing approaches for robot learning in simulation often require substantial manual effort to construct scenes and specify tasks, limiting training scalability and data diversity. Meanwhile, in-the-wild robot demonstrations naturally provide diverse and realistic observations of real-world interactions. Leveraging these demonstrations for simulation requires both high-fidelity visual reconstruction and physically consistent interactions. General-purpose agents offer flexible adaptation to diverse scenarios and strong reasoning about 3D spatial relationships, while specialized generative models provide high-fidelity reconstruction of scene appearance and geometry. We introduce WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework that constructs interactive digital twins from in-the-wild robot demonstrations. Our central idea is to formulate real-to-sim construction as the iterative refinement of an executable world program. A coding agent decomposes the observed scene, plans reconstruction steps, and orchestrates specialized image and 3D generation tools, refining the program through verification feedback. A camera-pose-anchored scene representation organizes the world into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships among the scene, objects, and robot. The agent uses this representation to diagnose and correct reconstruction errors, enabling physically consistent interaction and trajectory replay. Experiments on DROID demonstrate that WorldMirror can reconstruct visually faithful and geometrically consistent interactive worlds while preserving the physical validity of recorded robot trajectories.

具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).title: Robotic Spatiotemporal Editing: A Unified Interface for Controllable Action Generation via Masked Action Reconstruction
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).authors_text: Yanbang Li, Bu He, Yi Tian, Yu-Chiao Huang, Chenyu Zhang
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).summary: The paper presents the MAP interface for spatiotemporal control of robot actions, using an Inpainting Policy to unify and reconstruct action dimensions effectively.
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).debug_abstract: Generative policies can synthesize robot behaviors, yet controlling and editing them through diverse spatiotemporal references remains challenging. In the real world, human intent requires robot behaviors that satisfy constraints on where, when, and how actions are executed. Our key insight is that spatiotemporal control references, such as keypoints, flows, orientations, and keyposes, can be viewed as partial specifications of the same temporal Cartesian action space. We introduce the MAP (Masked Action Space) interface to unify these action references and formulate controllable manipulation as an action inpainting problem. Our Inpainting Policy (IP) reconstructs missing action dimensions of the end-effector, combining progress-guided alignment with multi-mask training supporting unseen action-constraint combinations. We further adopt a training-free RePaint variant that iteratively inpaints the action during denoising to reduce control error. On ManiSkill and LIBERO-10, our policy achieves average task success rates of 92.67% and 64.67%, respectively.Real-world experiments demonstrate spatiotemporal control with average positional and rotational errors of 44.3 mm and 7°, respectively, showing that our policy can use diverse references to guide executable robot behaviors.

具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).title: WAM-TTT: Steering World-Action Models by Watching Human Play at Test Time
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).authors_text: Yusen Feng, Bingchen Han, Jiangran Lyu, Kai Liu, Yixin Zheng
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).summary: WAM-TTT enables efficient adaptation of robot foundation models using unlabeled human videos at test time, enhancing performance without additional demonstrations or fine-tuning.
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).debug_abstract: Steering robot foundation models (RFMs) toward new task variants or user-preferred behaviors remains challenging, often requiring additional robot demonstrations, task-specific fine-tuning, or long-context conditioning. We present WAM-TTT, a test-time training framework for steering world action models from raw human videos. To make this memory useful for control, we introduce a meta-training stage that aligns human demonstrations with robot behaviors using paired human-robot data and a key--value memory reconstruction objective. At test time, only unlabeled human videos are required to adapt the memory, while the pretrained WAM remains frozen. This enables efficient and reusable steering without robot actions, human-side annotations, or task-specific fine-tuning, while preserving the generalization ability of the foundation model. Extensive experiments show that WAM-TTT consistently outperforms in-context human-video conditioning baselines across diverse manipulation tasks and generalization settings.

具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).title: Seeing Through the Chain: Understanding and Mitigating Hallucinations in Multimodal Large Reasoning Models
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).authors_text: Hao Fang, Jinyu Li, Jiawei Kong, Tianqu Zhuang, Kuofeng Gao
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).summary: This paper presents C3PO, a framework that mitigates hallucinations in multimodal reasoning models by enhancing reasoning quality and filtering redundant tokens for improved signal efficiency.
具身智能实验室 (TEA Lab).debug_abstract: While multimodal reasoning models (MLRMs) have exhibited impressive capabilities, they remain prone to hallucinations, and effective solutions are still underexplored. In this paper, we experimentally analyze the hallucination cause and propose C3PO, a training-based mitigation framework comprising \textbf{C}hain-of-Thought \textbf{C}ompression and \textbf{C}ontrastive \textbf{P}reference \textbf{O}ptimization. Firstly, we identify that introducing reasoning mechanisms exacerbates models' reliance on language priors while overlooking visual inputs, which can produce CoTs with reduced visual cues but redundant text tokens. In addition, we observe that the quality of the reasoning trace largely determines whether hallucination emerges in subsequent responses. To leverage this insight, we introduce a reasoning-enhanced preference tuning scheme that constructs training pairs using high-quality AI feedback. We further design a multimodal hallucination-inducing mechanism that elicits models' inherent hallucination patterns via carefully crafted inducers, yielding informative negative signals for contrastive correction. We provide theoretical justification for the effectiveness and demonstrate consistent hallucination reduction across diverse MLRMs and benchmarks.

MARS多模态学习实验室.title: Do Robotic World Models Really Follow Actions? Diagnosing and Aligning Action-Conditioned Generation for Policy Learning
MARS多模态学习实验室.authors_text: Sixiang Chen, Jiaming Liu, Jixian Wu, Yichen Guo, Tinghao Wang
MARS多模态学习实验室.summary: The paper introduces WorldEcho and WorldSync to evaluate and improve action-conditioned world models, enhancing their reliability for robotic policy learning by aligning generated futures with actual actions.
MARS多模态学习实验室.debug_abstract: Action-conditioned world models increasingly serve as learned simulators for robotic policy improvement, yet their reliability rests on an unverified assumption: generated futures faithfully reflect the consequences of arbitrary valid actions.
